Switching noise, especially simultaneous switching noise (SSN), is a major source of EMI in high-speed PCBs.
Power and ground planes in multilayer PCBs act as parallel-plate waveguides and microstrip patch antennas, radiating noise at board edges.
EBG structures can prevent propagation of electromagnetic surface waves within specific frequency bands, creating bandgaps.
High-impedance surfaces (HIS) are periodic structures of metallic patches connected by vias that create band-stop filters for EMI suppression.
A ribbon of HIS structures placed around PCB edges between power planes can effectively shield and reduce radiation.
Simulations show the HIS bandgap lies approximately between 4 GHz and 8 GHz for typical patch sizes of 5 mm.
Experimental PCB prototypes demonstrated about 30 dB average suppression of radiated noise from 4 to 10 GHz.
Cascading HIS structures with different patch sizes can create ultrawide-band suppression covering multiple frequency bands.
The bandgap frequency depends on patch size, via diameter and length, gap size, board thickness, and substrate permittivity.
Extending vias to the opposite plane with anti-pads and reducing board thickness does not significantly affect the bandgap.
The HIS structures can be fabricated using standard PCB manufacturing processes without significantly increasing board size.
The suppression technique is effective regardless of PCB power plane stack-up configuration (e.g., GVGV, GVVG).
Traditional EMI reduction methods like decoupling capacitors have limitations due to component inductance and cost.
The HIS method suppresses radiation caused by noise propagation between power planes rather than just edge fringing fields.
The experimental setup used a vector network analyzer and a monopole antenna to measure radiated emissions at multiple points.
The HIS structures provide omni-directional suppression of radiated noise around the PCB edges.
The technique can also suppress harmonics of switching noise frequencies by proper HIS design.
The HIS structures act as perfect magnetic conductors (PMC) over their bandgap frequency range.
The study is the first to apply EBG/HIS structures specifically for EMI reduction from PCB power buses.
The HIS structures reduce the effective radiation path by creating a low impedance path that shorts high-frequency currents at patch locations.
